## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet, and the starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds. In the code, it squeezes each column into a 2D embedding with 1x1 convs, then pools that over brick footprints. A brick lands one layer above the tallest column under its footprint, so a good placement needs every footprint cell to be missing at that one shared layer. Per-cell embeddings pooled with min, max and mean represent this poorly when column heights differ. My main idea is a layered head: a learned conv along the height axis gives features for each (layer, cell). Footprint pooling and scoring then happen per layer, and a logsumexp over layers combines them. Because every op is 2D, it stays cheap (r ≈ 1.2). The recipe uses 2 PPO epochs for more samples and a higher gamma and lambda for the end bonus. As a control, the third candidate is the starting architecture with the same recipe, which shows whether the recipe alone gives nonzero success.

### Round 2
All three trials scored 0 on dev and 0 on training success, including the recipe-only control. No signal favours any head yet. One cause is common to all three: very few policy updates. 256 envs × 16 steps = 4096 samples per update, so even 230k steps is only about 55 updates with the learning rate decaying to 0. That is very little policy iteration for exact builds, which need about 10 correct placements in a row and then a correct DONE. This round tests a recipe built for many updates: ppo_epochs 1 (about 2.6x more samples), 128 envs × 16 steps, and 64-sample minibatches. That gives about 200 updates and about 6,600 gradient steps instead of about 55 updates. The recipe is applied to three different networks: (A) the starting architecture; (B) a new, normalised residual all-convolutional net with a 3x3 per-type output head, which makes no assumptions about anchor or drop rules in case the world differs; (C) LayerFoot. If all three stay at 0 training success, the update count is not the bottleneck.

### Round 3
All six trials score exactly 0, on dev and also in training (last 10%). This holds across three architectures (start, LayerFoot, norm-ResNet), two epoch settings, gamma 0.95 and 0.99, and ent_coef 0.005 and 0.01. Architecture alone does not seem to be the bottleneck. A likely shared cause is the policy collapsing to an early DONE. Under a near-uniform policy, random placements mostly fill cells outside the target, so they earn negative reward, while DONE earns 0. Advantage-normalised PPO then quickly makes DONE dominant, exploration stops and success stays at 0. We cannot see episode lengths, but the result matches this. This round tests anti-collapse recipes (higher entropy, shorter horizon) on the cheap structured LayerFoot head and on the starting architecture. A third candidate adds a flat output path to the conv net that does not assume the action layout, in case this world indexes actions differently from its description. Any nonzero result is progress.

### Round 4
All 9 trials scored exactly 0 on dev and 0 in training, on both seeds each. The trials covered footprint-pooling heads, per-layer LayerFoot heads, a norm-ResNet conv head and a flat head, with 1, 2 or 4 PPO epochs, gamma from 0.9 to 0.99 and entropy from 0.005 to 0.03. Changing the recipe or the trunk shape never helped. These were quite different, reasonable designs, and every one failed completely. That points to a single shared assumption being wrong, more than to a lack of capacity or samples. The task warns that the world may not match its description. The assumption every spatial head shares is the action-index layout: type-major order, then y, then x, with the anchor at the top-left. If the real layout is transposed or type-minor, every conv head would assign scores to the wrong actions and could not learn. My last-round bet is a head that does not depend on the layout. It has one learned score map per candidate index order, all summed. The legal-action mask is also fed in under each of those orders. A flat linear path from global features to every action is added too, so DONE could be learned at any index.
